lessonTitle: General Approach to Poisoning: ABCDE, Activated Charcoal and Toxicology Advice

blocks.text: A 19-year-old is brought in by friends after a party. He is drowsy, his pupils are widely dilated, his skin is hot and dry, and his heart rate is 138 per minute. Nobody knows what he took. You cannot wait for a drug name; the pattern of signs and the order in which you act already guide the first minutes of care.

blocks.markdown: Poisoning is exposure to a substance in a quantity that causes harm. Management follows the same logic as any acutely unwell patient: treat life-threatening problems in order of priority, then gather the history, identify the agent, reduce absorption where this helps, give a specific antidote if one exists, and support the patient until the poison is eliminated. Most poisoned patients recover with good supportive care.

rows: Airway
Reduced consciousness, loss of gag, vomiting, burns from corrosives
Open and protect the airway; call for senior or anaesthetic help if the Glasgow Coma Scale score is 8 or less
Breathing
Respiratory depression, aspiration, bronchospasm, pulmonary oedema
Oxygen as needed, assess rate and saturation, support ventilation
Circulation
Hypotension, arrhythmia, prolonged QRS or QT intervals
Monitor, 12-lead ECG, intravenous access, fluids as indicated
Disability
Coma, seizures, hypoglycaemia, abnormal pupils
Check GCS, pupils and capillary glucose; treat seizures and low glucose
Exposure
Hyperthermia or hypothermia, skin contamination, signs of injection
Measure temperature, remove contaminated clothing, examine for toxidrome clues
blocks.caption: ABCDE assessment of a poisoned patient.

blocks.markdown: After stabilisation, take a focused history from patient, relatives, ambulance crew and containers: **what** was taken (name and formulation), **how much**, **when**, by which route, whether alcohol or other drugs were co-ingested, intent (accidental or deliberate), and the patient's medical history, age and weight. Examination can suggest a **toxidrome**, a cluster of signs typical of a class of poison.

rows: Anticholinergic
Dilated pupils, hot dry skin, tachycardia, urinary retention, agitation
Cholinergic (for example organophosphates)
Small pupils, salivation, lacrimation, diarrhoea, bronchorrhoea, bradycardia
Opioid
Reduced consciousness, small pupils, slow shallow breathing
Sympathomimetic
Tachycardia, hypertension, sweating, dilated pupils, hyperthermia
blocks.caption: Selected toxidromes.

blocks.title: Activated charcoal
blocks.text: Activated charcoal is a finely divided carbon with a large surface area that adsorbs many drugs in the gut, reducing absorption. A single adult dose is commonly 50 g, and a child dose is about 1 g/kg (teaching example, up to 50 g). It works best if given within about one hour of ingestion of a potentially toxic amount of an adsorbable substance.

rows: Recent (within about 1 hour) ingestion of a significant quantity of a toxic substance that charcoal binds
Unprotected or compromised airway, reduced consciousness (aspiration risk)
Patient alert and able to protect the airway, or airway secured by intubation
Intestinal obstruction, ileus or perforation
Substance known to be adsorbed (for example carbamazepine, theophylline, many tricyclic drugs)
Corrosives, hydrocarbons (aspiration) and substances that charcoal does not bind well, such as iron, lithium, alcohols and strong acids or alkalis
blocks.caption: Decision guide for activated charcoal. Always confirm with local toxicology advice.

blocks.title: Is activated charcoal still appropriate?
blocks.prompt: A 30-year-old alert man took a potentially toxic amount of an adsorbable drug at 14:10 and arrives in the emergency department at 15:40. He is protecting his airway. Decide whether to give charcoal.

steps.text: Compute the time since ingestion: 14:10 to 15:40 is 1 hour 30 minutes (90 minutes).
The usual window is about 1 hour, so he is outside it, although absorption can be delayed with some preparations or large overdoses.
He has no contraindication, but benefit is uncertain; the decision should be guided by the toxicology information service.

blocks.answer: Beyond the usual 1-hour window: charcoal is not routinely indicated and would be given only on specialist advice, for example for a delayed-absorption formulation.

blocks.markdown: **Toxicology information services.** Services such as TOXBASE and the National Poisons Information Service in the United Kingdom, and poison control centres elsewhere, provide current, specific advice on the toxicity, features, investigations and treatment of thousands of agents. Use them early for unfamiliar agents, uncertain doses, multiple ingestants or when treatment decisions depend on dose or time. Have ready the agent and formulation (including whether modified-release), the amount, the time, the patient's age, weight and comorbidity, co-ingestants and the current clinical findings. Document the advice and the person giving it, follow up as advised and re-check if the situation changes.

blocks.latex: \text{Dose ingested (mg/kg)}=\frac{\text{number of tablets}\times\text{mg per tablet}}{\text{body weight (kg)}}
blocks.caption: Dose per kilogram is compared with the toxic threshold given by the information service.

blocks.title: Estimating mg/kg ingested
blocks.prompt: A 14 kg child may have swallowed up to 6 tablets, each of 25 mg, of a drug (hypothetical teaching example). Calculate the maximum dose in mg/kg.
blocks.answer: About 10.7 mg/kg; compare with the toxic threshold from the information service.

blocks.title: Treat the patient, not the story
blocks.text: The history may be unreliable. Assume the worst plausible exposure until shown otherwise, reassess repeatedly, and avoid measures such as induced vomiting, which are not recommended.

points: Use ABCDE for the poisoned patient, protecting the airway first, and check glucose and temperature; toxidromes help identify the class of poison.

Activated charcoal is indicated early after ingestion of adsorbable toxic amounts in a patient who protects the airway, and contraindicated by unprotected airway, obstruction, corrosives or hydrocarbons and by non-adsorbed substances.
Use toxicology information services early, with the agent, amount, time and patient details ready.

questions.stem: In the initial assessment of a poisoned patient, which problem takes priority?

options.text: Obtaining a full history from relatives

distractorRationale.a: Correct: A comes first in ABCDE.
distractorRationale.c: Identification should not delay life-saving care.

questions.explanation: Airway obstruction is the most immediately life-threatening problem, so it is secured first. History and antidotes follow once vital functions are supported.

questions.stem: A poisoned patient has a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 7, is snoring and has vomited. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Open and protect the airway and call for senior or anaesthetic help

questions.correctOptionText: Open and protect the airway and call for senior or anaesthetic help

distractorRationale.b: Charcoal is contraindicated with an unprotected airway.
distractorRationale.c: Waiting risks death from obstruction or aspiration.

questions.explanation: GCS of 8 or less implies the airway may be unprotected. The airway must be secured before other interventions.

questions.stem: A patient has dilated pupils, hot dry skin, tachycardia and urinary retention. Which toxidrome is this?

distractorRationale.b: Cholinergic gives small pupils and secretions.
distractorRationale.d: Sedatives do not cause this autonomic pattern.

questions.explanation: Blockade of muscarinic receptors causes mydriasis, dry skin, tachycardia and urinary retention. Recognising the toxidrome directs supportive care.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old alert man swallowed a large quantity of an adsorbable drug 30 minutes ago and can protect his airway. What is a reasonable option?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: within the window, alert, adsorbable.

questions.explanation: Charcoal is most effective within about an hour for adsorbable drugs when the airway is protected.

questions.stem: For which ingestion is activated charcoal contraindicated?

options.text: A hydrocarbon such as a petrol-type solvent
A tricyclic antidepressant taken 40 minutes ago by an alert patient
Carbamazepine taken 30 minutes ago by an alert patient
Theophylline taken 45 minutes ago by an alert patient

questions.correctOptionText: A hydrocarbon such as a petrol-type solvent

distractorRationale.a: Correct: aspiration risk and poor adsorption.

questions.explanation: Hydrocarbons cause severe pneumonitis if aspirated and are not well adsorbed. The other agents are bound by charcoal.

questions.stem: Before contacting a toxicology information service, it is helpful to know the agent, the amount, the time of ingestion and the patient's age and weight.
questions.explanation: Management advice depends on dose per kilogram and time since ingestion. Having the data ready makes advice quicker and more accurate.

questions.stem: A 70 kg adult may have taken 40 tablets of 250 mg of a drug (hypothetical teaching example). Calculate the maximum dose ingested in mg/kg to report to the information service.
questions.explanation: The total is 40 x 250 = 10 000 mg. Dividing by 70 kg gives about 142.9 mg/kg.

questions.stem: A 22 kg child is judged suitable for a single dose of activated charcoal at 1 g/kg (teaching example, maximum 50 g). Calculate the dose in g.
questions.explanation: The dose is 1 g/kg times 22 kg, which is 22 g. This is below the 50 g maximum.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old is found drowsy after an unknown ingestion. Outline an ABCDE-based initial assessment and what you would check at each step.
markingGuide: Airway: patency, protect if GCS 8 or less
Circulation: pulse, blood pressure, ECG monitoring, access
Disability: GCS, pupils, capillary glucose, seizures
Exposure: temperature, skin, signs of injection or toxidrome
Treat life threats as they are found
Then history, containers and information service
questions.explanation: ABCDE prioritises life-threatening problems in order, and poisoning adds specific checks such as glucose, ECG and temperature.

questions.stem: State the indications and contraindications for activated charcoal and explain how you would use a toxicology information service in managing an overdose of an unfamiliar tablet.
markingGuide: Indication: recent significant ingestion of an adsorbable toxic substance, ideally within about 1 hour
Patient must protect the airway or have it secured
Contraindication: unprotected airway or reduced consciousness
Contraindication: corrosives, hydrocarbons and non-adsorbed substances such as iron or lithium
Contact the service with agent, formulation, amount, time, weight and clinical state
questions.explanation: Charcoal reduces absorption but carries aspiration risk. Information services give agent-specific, up-to-date advice and marking should reward the data needed.
